kinds.invented: a byline found by a publisher or platform not to belong to a real writer
kinds.impersonated: a real writer whose name an impostor used
kinds.fake_expert: an invented expert quoted as a source

note: Only cases a publisher, platform or the impersonated writer has documented in public, each with its sources. Real people share these names: a match means verify, never fake. outlets lists where the byline or expert appeared; domain is null when no source confirms it. reported is the month the case was first reported.

cases.name: Caroline Williams
cases.what: a real science journalist. In 2026 an impostor used her name and clips to sell Science a story, which Science removed three months later, and then pitched Science and Knowable again.

cases.name: Katie Campbell
cases.what: a real KUOW reporter. In 2026 scammers used her name and Gmail addresses made to look like KUOW's to email book authors, then asked them to pay for interviews.

cases.name: Ruth Jackson-Kirby
cases.what: a real UK personal-finance journalist. In 2026 an impostor pitched FinanceBuzz from an address resembling hers, citing her work history; FinanceBuzz ran articles under her name with an author page showing an AI photo, then took her name and the page down when she objected.

cases.name: Eleni Nicolaou
cases.what: an art-therapist persona, 'Dr Eleni Nicolaou', quoted more than 30 times in 2026 by outlets including Forbes, Vice, Glamour, Tom's Guide and Parade; Press Gazette found she appeared to be AI-generated, and Qwoted removed her profile.

cases.name: Jacob Elban
cases.what: a 'business expert' persona offered to journalists by the same company as 'Dr Eleni Nicolaou'; Qwoted and Pressflow removed his profile in September 2026 over doubts that he was real.
